front_blocks.md: Define the **net realisable value** of inventory.

back_blocks.md: The **net realisable value** is the amount a business expects to receive from selling the goods, after the costs of selling them.
It is the **selling price minus any selling expenses**, such as repairs to damaged goods.

front_blocks.md: Complete the sentence about the cost of inventory:
The cost of inventory is the purchase cost of the goods plus the cost of `\_\_\_\_\_\_`.

back_blocks.md: The completed sentence is:
The cost of inventory is the purchase cost of the goods plus the cost of **carriage inwards**.

front_blocks.md: At what value is inventory shown in the financial statements?

back_blocks.md: At the **lower** of its cost and its net realisable value.
This follows the principle of **prudence**, so that neither the asset nor the profit is overstated.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Inventory is normally valued at its net realisable value.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
For most inventory the **cost** is the lower of the two figures, so the cost is what is normally used. Net realisable value takes over only in particular cases.

front_blocks.md: When is the net realisable value lower than the cost?

back_blocks.md: When goods have been **damaged** and need repair before they can be sold, when they are **close to their expiry date**, or when they are being sold cheaply to **promote a new product**.

cards.front_md: When is the net realisable value lower than the cost?

front_blocks.md: An item cost \$15 plus \$3 delivery, and after \$8 of repairs it could be sold for \$24. What is its inventory value?

back_blocks.md: The cost is \$15 + \$3 = \$18 and the net realisable value is \$24 − \$8 = \$16, and inventory takes the lower of the two.

cards.front_md: An item cost \$15 plus \$3 delivery, and after \$8 of repairs it could be sold for \$24. What is its inventory value?
cards.back_md:
**\$16.**

The cost is \$15 + \$3 = \$18 and the net realisable value is \$24 − \$8 = \$16, and inventory takes the lower of the two.

front_blocks.md: How do you value an inventory made up of several different items?

back_blocks.md: Compare the cost and the net realisable value **for each item separately**, take the lower figure, and multiply it by the number of units.
Adding those item totals together gives the valuation of the whole inventory.

front_blocks.md: How does the value of the closing inventory affect the profit?

back_blocks.md: A higher closing inventory gives a **higher** profit.
The closing inventory is **subtracted** from the cost of sales, so a larger figure makes the cost of sales smaller.

front_blocks.md: How does the value of the opening inventory affect the profit?

back_blocks.md: A higher opening inventory gives a **lower** profit.
The opening inventory is **added** to the cost of sales, so a larger figure makes the cost of sales bigger.

back_blocks.md: The completed sentence is:
If the closing inventory is overvalued, the gross profit and the profit for the year are both **overstated**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
An error in the opening inventory affects the assets in the statement of financial position.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
The opening inventory does not appear in the statement of financial position at all. Only the **closing** inventory does, under current assets.

front_blocks.md: The opening inventory has been undervalued. What is the effect on the profit for the year?

back_blocks.md: Both the gross profit and the profit for the year are **overstated**.
Too little has been added to the cost of sales, so the cost of sales comes out too low.

front_blocks.md: The closing inventory has been overvalued. What is the effect on the statement of financial position?

back_blocks.md: Both the **assets** and the **capital** are **overstated**.
The closing inventory is a current asset, and the profit it has overstated is carried into the capital.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
An inventory error changes the gross profit and the profit for the year by the same amount.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
The error sits in the **cost of sales**, which feeds into both figures, so the two move in the same direction and by the same amount.

front_blocks.md: Why does an error in the opening inventory leave the capital at the end of the year unaffected?

back_blocks.md: Because the same figure was the previous year's closing inventory, so it distorted that year's profit in the **opposite** direction.
The two errors cancel, and the closing capital is correct even though each year's profit was wrong.
